weeks.title: The Church Is the Body of Christ
weeks.keyText: Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.
weeks.theme: I am not a spectator sitting in church; I am an indispensable member of Christ’s body.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 12:12-27. Which sentence moves you most, and why?
Have you ever felt that you didn’t really matter at church? How does God’s Word change that view?
Which member of your small group will you reach out to and care for this week? Name one specific thing you will do.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, pause before you walk into the sanctuary and tell the Lord, “I’m not here to watch a service; I’m here to worship together with your body.” During the service, notice someone you usually overlook. Afterward, go and greet them, and write down their name so you can pray for them.

lessons.title: One Body, Many Members
lessons.hear:
When many people hear the word “church,” what comes to mind is a building, a Sunday service, a weekly bulletin. But the first picture Paul paints of the church is not a house; it is a body: “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12).

Notice that last phrase—“so also is Christ.” Paul doesn’t say “so also is the church”; he says “Christ.” The church is so closely united with Christ that Paul simply calls this body by Christ’s own name. When Saul was persecuting believers, the risen Lord stopped him on the road to Damascus and asked, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). To persecute the church is to persecute Christ himself.

A body has three characteristics. First, it is alive, not assembled. Its members are not spare parts glued on afterward; they grow out of one and the same life. Second, it is united but not uniform. Eyes, ears, hands, and feet are all different, yet they belong to one body. Third, it has a head. Life, direction, and every command come from the head.

So the day you became a Christian, you were not only “saved”—you were also placed into a body. You may not have found your place yet, but you are already a member. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes, so that you no longer see church as somewhere you “go,” but see yourself as someone who is “in the body.”
lessons.light: A self-centered person looks at a church and asks, “Is this church right for me?” A selfless person asks, “The Lord has placed me in this body—how does he want me to work together with the others?” Change begins with our mindset: when I shift from a human perspective to God’s perspective, I am no longer a customer shopping for a product but a member placed by the Lord.
think: In 1 Corinthians 12:12-20, which parts of the body does Paul use as illustrations?
When I say I’m “going to church,” what picture comes to mind?
If the church is the body of Christ, how can I live out my identity as a member this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for placing me in your body. Forgive me for so often treating the church as a venue, a program, even a place to find fault. Holy Spirit, open my eyes to see that I am a member of your body, and that the brothers and sisters beside me are fellow members with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the names of three brothers and sisters from your church (or small group). Beside each name, write: “They are the body of Christ, and we belong to one body.” Then pray one sentence for each of them.
lessons.quick: Church is not a place I go; it is the body I belong to.
text: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.
For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.
For the body is not one member, but many.
If the foot would say, “Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body,” it is not therefore not part of the body.
If the ear would say, “Because I’m not the eye, I’m not part of the body,” it’s not therefore not part of the body.
If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?
But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.
If they were all one member, where would the body be?
But now they are many members, but one body.

lessons.title: “I Have No Need for You”?
lessons.hear:
A brother who had been in church for more than ten years once said, “I just need to come on Sundays and hear the sermon. Small group takes too much time, and serving—let other people do that.” He wasn’t a bad person; he simply treated church like a gas station: pull in when you’re running low, fill up, and drive off. Then one day he was hospitalized for surgery and lay in a hospital bed for three weeks without anyone knowing. After he was discharged, he wept as he told his pastor, for the first time, “I’ve just realized I never belonged to anyone.”

Paul writes, “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). In the Corinthian church, some felt their gifts were so great and their standing so high that they didn’t need anyone else. Others felt so unimpressive that they concluded, “Because I’m not the hand, I’m not part of the body.” These two attitudes look like opposites, but they spring from the same source: both measure their relationship to the body with self at the center.

God’s perspective is completely different: “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary” (1 Corinthians 12:22). In God’s design, no member is superfluous, and no member can survive on its own. A finger cut off from the hand, however nimble it once was, will wither and die.

Ask yourself honestly: Am I the eye that says, “I have no need for you”? Or am I the foot that says, “I’m not part of the body”? Both need to repent and return to the place God has arranged for us.
lessons.light: Pride says, “I have no need for you.” Insecurity says, “You have no need for me.” Both mean leaving our proper place. Humility is not thinking very little of yourself; it is seeing yourself the way God does: I need you, and you need me. This is the selfless life—not centered on myself, but mindful of the body of Christ.
think: In 1 Corinthians 12:21-27, how does God treat the members that seem “weaker” or “less honorable”?
Am I more like the eye that says, “I have no need for you,” or the foot that says, “I’m not part of the body”?
Is there a member I have overlooked, someone I felt I had “no need for”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often think I can live out my faith on my own, without needing others and without wanting to be needed. Break both the pride and the insecurity in me. Help me see the place you have arranged for me, and value every member of the body. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a brother or sister you have paid little attention to in the past. Today, send them a message: “How have you been? I prayed for you.” It doesn’t need to be long—just sincere.
lessons.quick: No member is superfluous—not me, and not you.
text: The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.”
No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.
Those parts of the body which we think to be less honorable, on those we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable parts have more abundant modesty,
while our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part,
that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another.
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.

lessons.title: A Body That Cares for One Another
lessons.hear:
The human body has a wonderful design. When you stub your toe on the leg of a table, your whole body instantly bends over, your hand reaches for your foot, your eyes check the injury, and your mouth lets out an “Ouch!” No one calls a meeting to decide whether to help the toe; the whole body simply moves together. Paul says the church should be like that: “that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:25-26).

Caring for one another is not the job of a few zealous ministry team members; it is the instinct of every member. Often it is very ordinary: remembering that a sister has a job interview this week and texting her a prayer; noticing that an elderly man always eats alone after the service and inviting him to your table; hearing that a family has just moved and bringing them a meal.

Today’s assignment is simple: find a member who is suffering or celebrating, and be “with” them. Weeping with those who weep doesn’t mean handing them a pile of principles; rejoicing with those who rejoice doesn’t mean quietly comparing yourself with them. Paul gives the same instruction in Romans: “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

When you do this, you are practicing a truth: I do not follow Christ on my own; I live within a body.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A body’s health is not measured by how lively its events are, but by whether its members are truly “with” one another. A church where Jesus reigns will naturally grow a life of mutual care; this is the fruit of the Spirit, not a system imposed by rules.
think: What two kinds of being “with” one another does 1 Corinthians 12:25-26 mention?
Has a member recently been suffering or honored, and I was not “with” them?
What concrete way can I be “with” them today?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me a heart that can feel. Don’t let me sit numbly through services any longer; help me notice the pain and the joy of the members around me. Lead me today to the one you want me to care for, and help me love them with your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose a member who is going through a hardship or celebrating good news. Give them a call, bring them a small treat, or visit in person—and pray for them, face to face or over the phone.
lessons.quick: When one member suffers, the whole body suffers—and I choose to be “with” them.
text: while our presentable parts have no such need. But God composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part,
that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another.
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

lessons.title: Where the Head Leads, the Body Follows
lessons.hear:
No matter how strong a body is, if its head is confused, it will stumble around aimlessly. Paul says God “gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all” (Ephesians 1:22-23). The church’s greatest problem is often not a shortage of talent or resources, but that something else has taken over the place of the head.

Sometimes that place is occupied by a forceful leader, and everyone reads his expression before doing anything. Sometimes it is a large extended family—whoever has the most relatives gets the final say. Sometimes it is tradition: “We’ve always done it this way.” Most hidden of all, it is me—my preferences, my reputation, my opinions. When one member tries to direct the whole body, the body goes into spasm.

Today, quietly examine yourself: In the way I take part in church life, who is acting as the head? When I’m unhappy with a sermon, disagree with a decision, or dislike a certain co-worker, is my first reaction to seek the Lord’s heart—or to voice my feelings and find someone to complain to?

Self-examination is not for condemnation but for correction. And the way to correct course is actually quite simple: give the place of the head back to Christ. Every time you are about to voice an opinion about church matters, first ask three questions: Is this what Jesus wants? Is it in line with the Bible? Is this the prompting of the Holy Spirit, or just my emotions?
lessons.light: The self-centered life wants to be the head; the selfless life gladly serves as a member. Pride is leaving our proper place as a member and grasping the power that belongs to the Head alone. To let Jesus reign, in the most concrete terms of church life, means this: my opinions must bow to the will of the Head.
think: What does Ephesians 1:20-23 say about Christ’s position? What is the relationship between the church and Christ?
In what areas of church life do I want to be the “head”?
The next time I have an opinion about the church, what will I do first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the head of the church, and you are my head. I confess that I often want my own opinions to rule, judging your church by my own likes and dislikes. Today I give the place of the head back to you. Reign in my heart, and guide my words and my attitude. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: In your journal, write down one recent thing about your church that you’ve been “unhappy” about. Bring it before the Lord and honestly ask, “Lord, how do you see this? How should I respond?” Then write down one sentence you receive from the Holy Spirit.
lessons.quick: When I give the place of the head back to Christ, I return to my proper place as a member.
text: which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places,
far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come.
He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly,
which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

lessons.title: Built Up in Love
lessons.hear:
This week we started with a simple picture: the church is the body of Christ. Now let’s turn it over in our hearts again and again, chew on it slowly, and then pass it on to someone else.

Paul describes what a healthy body looks like. Christ is the head, “from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:16). Notice a few key phrases. “From whom”—life comes from Christ. “Each individual part”—everyone has a place. “Every joint supplies”—no one goes it alone. “In love”—all the building happens in an atmosphere of love.

Imagine an orchestra. The violin doesn’t need to envy the timpani, and the flute has no reason to look down on the bassoon. As long as every player keeps their eyes on the same conductor and follows the same score, their different sounds blend into beautiful harmony. The church is beautiful not because everyone is the same, but because different people work together under the leading of one Lord.

To multiply means to tell someone else the truth you received this week. You don’t need to preach a sermon or teach a class—just share one simple sentence: “This week I discovered that I don’t just go to church; I am part of the church.” And when one more person begins to see themselves this way, the church gains one more member who has woken up.
lessons.light: The last of the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication. Truth that stops with me is like a blocked artery in the body; only when it flows out does it bring life. The practice of 920 begins with the “2” right beside you: today, pass on what you have received to someone you have a relationship with.
think: According to Ephesians 4:16, what does the body need in order to grow?
How has my view of “church” changed this week?
With whom will I share what I received this week, and when?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for showing me this week that I am a member of the body of Christ. Let this truth take root in my heart and pass through me to others. May our church be built up in love, each part doing its work and helping one another, so that Christ receives the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find your spiritual companion or someone in your small group. Spend five minutes sharing the verse that moved you most this week, invite them to share their thoughts too, and then pray for each other.
lessons.quick: Each part doing its share, helping one another, built up together in love.
text: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.

weeks.title: The Church Is God’s Family
weeks.keyText: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,
weeks.theme: I am no longer a guest at church; I am a child in God’s family, a brother or sister to God’s people.
group: Read Ephesians 2:13-19. How does Paul describe our change from “strangers” to “family”?
At church, are you more like a guest, a tenant, or family? Why?
Which member of your small group will you treat as family this week? Name one specific thing you will do.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before you leave home, pray for the brothers and sisters in God’s family, the way you think of your relatives on your way back home for a visit. During the service, greet an older member as you would your own parent, and give a young person a word of encouragement as you would a younger sibling. Afterward, don’t rush off—stay and help tidy up, the way family does.

lessons.title: From Foreigners to Family
lessons.hear:
Most of us know the feeling. You visit a friend’s home, and no matter how warm the host is, you still sit carefully on the edge of the sofa. When you finish your drink, you don’t know where to put the cup, and you ask before doing anything at all. However welcome a guest may be, a guest is still a guest. But when you get back to your own home, you open the fridge without asking, lie down when you’re tired, and wash the dishes when you see them sitting in the sink. Home is the place you belong to without asking permission—and the place you naturally take responsibility for.

Paul told the Gentile believers in Ephesus that they had once been “separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of the promise” (Ephesians 2:12). But the cross changed everything. Christ “broke down the middle wall of separation” (Ephesians 2:14), so that now, as Paul says of those far and near alike, “through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). And so he concludes: “So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

Notice that the way into this household is not a membership earned by good performance, but the blood of Christ. We were not merely “permitted to attend”; we were born into this family: “But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

Long ago, the psalmist glimpsed God’s heart: “God sets the lonely in families” (Psalm 68:6). That promise is fulfilled in the church. Perhaps you were never truly loved in the family you grew up in. Perhaps you are working hard, all alone, in a foreign land. Perhaps you are a new believer and everything still feels unfamiliar. Today, hear your heavenly Father say to you: You are not a guest. You have come home. Ask the Holy Spirit to make this more than something you know in your head—let your heart experience it: I belong to God’s household.
lessons.light: A self-centered person is a guest at church: satisfied when well served, gone when displeased. A selfless person is family at church: not only enjoying the warmth of home but also sharing its responsibilities. A changed mindset changes a life—when I move from “Which church should I go to?” to “Which household of God do I belong to?” my relationships with brothers and sisters move from politeness to kinship.
think: In Ephesians 2:13-19, what made those who were “far off” members of God’s household?
At church, is my posture more like a guest’s or a family member’s?
What small thing that “only family would do” can I do today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that through the blood of Jesus you broke down the dividing wall and brought me, who was far from you, back home. Forgive me for so often acting like a guest in your house—wanting to be served, unwilling to take responsibility. Holy Spirit, let me know deep in my heart that I am your child and that my brothers and sisters are my family. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: After the service this Sunday, don’t rush off. Do something only family would do: stack chairs, tidy up the refreshments, or spend ten minutes talking with a newcomer who is standing alone.
lessons.quick: I am not a guest in God’s house; I am a child brought home by the blood of Jesus.
text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ.
For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,
having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace,
and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.
He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.
For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.
So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,

lessons.title: Who Are My Brothers and Sisters?
lessons.hear:
A sister who grew up in the church said she had always treated it like a faith-based club: if she clicked with someone, she spent more time with them; if not, she kept her distance. Then her father passed away. Only a few relatives came from afar, but the brothers and sisters from her small group took turns keeping vigil with her through the nights, helped her handle matters large and small, and brought her three meals a day. She said, “Those few days, I finally realized I have a family at church.”

Deep down we often hold on to an old idea: family is about blood, and church is an organization; family is for life, while the people at church are just “people I know.” But Jesus’ words overturn that idea. When his mother and brothers stood outside calling for him, “looking around at those who sat around him, he said, ‘Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother’” (Mark 3:34-35).

Jesus was not belittling his earthly family—even on the cross he entrusted his mother to the disciple he loved (see John 19:26-27). He was declaring a deeper reality: in God’s kingdom there is a bond thicker than blood, shared by those who are born of the same heavenly Father and who together do his will. The Lord also promised that those who leave everything for him “will receive one hundred times more now in this time: houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children” (Mark 10:30). That hundredfold family is found in the church.

So the loud old uncle sitting next to you, the young person who is always late, the co-worker you don’t particularly admire—they are not merely “so-and-so from church.” They are your brothers and sisters. You didn’t choose them, just as you didn’t choose your own siblings. But your heavenly Father chose all of you and made you one family.
lessons.light: Self-centered relationships are handpicked: only those who suit me count as “my people.” Selfless relationships are received: whoever the Father gives me is my family. This is where the practice of 920 begins—every brother and sister the Father places beside me is one of my “2.” I don’t have to like someone first before I start loving them.
think: In Mark 3:31-35, how does Jesus redefine “family”?
Is there someone at church I treat only as an acquaintance rather than as family?
What word or action could I use to say, “You are my family”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for saying that whoever does God’s will is your brother, sister, and mother. I confess that I often use my own preferences to pick who counts as my people. Open my eyes to see the large family the Father has prepared for me, and teach me to accept and treasure the brothers and sisters I didn’t choose but you have given. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone at church you only nod to in passing. Today, send them a message to say hello, and ask a question about their life (their work, their family, or how they’ve been). Write down their answer and pray for them.
lessons.quick: The brothers and sisters the Father gives me are my family—not mine to pick.
text: His mother and his brothers came, and standing outside, they sent to him, calling him.
A multitude was sitting around him, and they told him, “Behold, your mother, your brothers, and your sisters are outside looking for you.”
He answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
Looking around at those who sat around him, he said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers!
For whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother.”

lessons.title: Treat One Another as Family
lessons.hear:
When Paul taught young Timothy how to relate to people in the church, he didn’t hand him a management manual. Instead he painted a picture of a family: “Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers; the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:1-2).

These two verses give us four relationships and two kinds of heart. Toward those older than us, we owe the respect we give our parents: even when we see things differently, we are never dismissive or mocking. Toward peers and those younger than us, we show the warmth of siblings: we can speak frankly without wounding. The final phrase, “in all purity,” matters too—closeness within a family must have holy boundaries, especially between men and women. A true home is a place where people feel safe.

Treating the church as family usually comes down to ordinary little things. One small group leader noticed that an elderly man in the group, who lived alone, spent every Lunar New Year eating by himself. So that year, several families in the group took turns inviting him over for the holiday meals. He said afterward that it was the first time in many years he had felt he’d come home. A university student studying overseas received a text from an auntie at church every week: “Have you eaten yet?” That one simple line carried him through his loneliest first year.

Paul also says, “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith” (Galatians 6:10). Today’s assignment is to choose an older member or a young person at church and treat them the way you would treat family. It doesn’t have to be anything big—just one thing you would do for your own parents or younger siblings.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A church with only programs and procedures is like a tidy but cold hotel; it becomes a home when people treat one another with family affection. A household where Jesus reigns is not held together by rules but by each person selflessly going one step further, asking one more question, saving one more seat.
think: What four relationships does 1 Timothy 5:1-2 mention, and with what attitude should each be treated?
Toward the older and younger people at church, is my attitude more like family or like a stranger?
Whom will I treat as family today, and what will I do?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you have placed me in a family with elders, peers, and young people. Teach me to respect older members as my parents and to treat younger ones warmly as my siblings, and keep me pure in every relationship. Lead me today to love the one you want me to love, so that they feel the warmth of your house. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose an older member or a young person at church and do one thing you would do for family: call to check in, invite them for a meal, bring them a small treat, or walk part of the way home with them.
lessons.quick: Treat elders as parents and the young as siblings, and the church becomes a home.
text: Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers;
the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity.

lessons.title: The Elder Son Who Stayed Home
lessons.hear:
In the parable of the prodigal son, people usually focus on the younger son who ran away from home and overlook the other lost son—the elder brother, who never left. He had labored in the fields for years. When he heard music and dancing at the house, “he was angry, and would not go in” (Luke 15:28). He told his father, “Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours” (Luke 15:29), and then complained that his brother had squandered the family’s wealth. Notice that he doesn’t say “my brother”; he says “this your son.”

Here is someone who lives in the house but lacks the heart of family. He treats his relationship with his father like employment: whatever I put in, I should get back. He sees his brother as a rival, not as a sibling who was lost and is found.

Those who have served in church for many years especially need to pause before this mirror. One long-serving ministry team member admitted that when a young newcomer was quickly entrusted with an important role, his first thought was not to thank God but, “I’ve served for so many years—why has no one noticed me?” In that moment, though he was at church every day, his heart was standing outside the door.

Take a quiet moment to examine yourself: In God’s house, am I a child or a hired hand? When others receive grace, are valued, and are welcomed, can I rejoice with them? Have I ever referred to a brother or sister as “that person” or “that crowd of theirs”?

The way to correct course lies in the father’s reply: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). What the elder son lacked was not a reward; he needed to see that he already had his father’s love. When I rest again in the Father’s love, I no longer need to compete with my brothers and sisters for favor, and I can walk into the house and celebrate with them.
lessons.light: The self-centered person in God’s house keeps score of merits and compares treatment, standing outside the door in anger like the elder son. The selfless person knows that everything is grace, and so can celebrate with those who were lost and are found. Pride leaves a child’s proper place and acts like a hired hand demanding wages; humility returns to that proper place and rests in the Father’s love.
think: In Luke 15:25-32, how does the elder son refer to his brother? And how does the father address him?
Has someone else’s blessing recently left a bitter taste in my mouth?
How can I rest in the Father’s love and once again call that person “my brother” or “my sister”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I am sometimes like that elder son—serving in your house while my heart keeps score, compares, and even stands outside the door in anger. Thank you for coming out yourself to plead with me and reminding me that I am always with you and all that is yours is mine. Heal my heart of competing for favor, so that I can celebrate with my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down the name of a member whose blessing has recently left you feeling sour. Offer a prayer of blessing for them to God, and this week look for a chance to sincerely congratulate them on the grace they have received.
lessons.quick: Living in God’s house is not enough; I need a child’s heart and a sibling’s love.
text: “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

lessons.title: God’s Family Needs Spiritual Parents
lessons.hear:
Paul explains why he is writing to Timothy: “that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). This week we began with “I have come home.” We saw that the Father has given us a large family, learned to treat one another as family, and recognized the shadow of the elder son in ourselves. Now let’s let these lessons take root, and pass them on.

A healthy family has not only brothers and sisters but also parents and children. Paul told the Corinthians, “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News” (1 Corinthians 4:15). Tutors teach you knowledge; parents give you life, walk with you as you grow, and pour themselves out for you. Today’s church has no shortage of speakers and courses, but it often lacks spiritual parents who are willing to spend time walking alongside people.

This is the “3” in the 235 of the 321 Vision: building relationships of spiritual parents and children. Spiritual parents are not meant to control their children’s lives or demand absolute obedience. Like Paul, they are “again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). The goal of good parents is for their children to grow up and eventually become parents to others.

So in God’s family, multiplication has a beautiful name: raising children. Think about it: Who are the spiritual parents who helped me grow? I can tell them thank you. And who around me needs an older brother or sister—or even a spiritual parent? You don’t have to wait until you are very mature. If you are just one step ahead, you can take their hand and walk with them.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 stands for relationships of spiritual parents and children. Selfless spiritual parents don’t build their own little circles; they help their children turn toward Christ. Selfless spiritual children don’t lean on people; they learn to stand while being supported. When life shapes life, God’s family is passed on from generation to generation.
think: How does 1 Timothy 3:15 describe God’s household, and what is its function?
Who has walked with me in my faith like a parent? Have I ever thanked them?
Which younger or newer member am I willing to begin walking alongside this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting me be loved and accompanied in your family, and thank you for the spiritual elders you sent to support me. Make me a blessing to others too—not controlling but accompanying, not building myself up but helping people become more like Jesus. Let your family flourish from generation to generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Do two things today: send a message of thanks to a spiritual elder who helped you grow, and invite a newer member to have coffee or chat online for fifteen minutes this week. Listen to their story and pray for them.
lessons.quick: God’s family needs more than speakers; it needs spiritual parents who help others grow.
text: These things I write to you, hoping to come to you shortly,
but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.

Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.

weeks.title: A Spiritual House of Living Stones
weeks.keyText: You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
weeks.theme: I am a living stone, precious to the Lord, being built together with my brothers and sisters into God’s dwelling place.
group: Read 1 Peter 2:4-10. What new understanding do the pictures of “living stones” and a “spiritual house” give you?
What in church life makes you feel God is “chiseling” you right now? How are you responding?
In what area of service will you work alongside another member this week, fitted together well?
weeks.sunday: As you walk into the sanctuary this Sunday, remind yourself: God doesn’t live in this building; he lives among us, the people he has called. During the service, notice the people sitting around you—each one is a living stone being built together with you. Afterward, pray for one of them, asking God to join you together and build you up as one.

lessons.title: Coming to the Living Stone
lessons.hear:
If you walk into an old stone church, you’ll notice that every stone is different: some large, some small, some neatly squared, some jagged. Yet laid together, they become a house that shelters people from wind and rain and welcomes them in to worship. Peter uses this picture to describe the church—but he isn’t talking about dead stones. He is talking about living ones.

Peter first points to Jesus: “a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious” (1 Peter 2:4). This stone was foretold long ago in the Old Testament: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). People saw Jesus as a failure, a reject; God made him the cornerstone of the whole building, the standard for every line, every angle, and all its stability.

Then Peter says, “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). Notice three things. First, we become living stones by “Come to him” (1 Peter 2:4); our life comes from him, not from ourselves. Second, we “are built up”—God is the builder; we don’t pile ourselves up. Third, stones are not there to be put on display and admired; they are meant to become a spiritual house where God dwells and people worship.

This is the mystery of the church: God’s presence is no longer confined to the temple in Jerusalem; he dwells among a people who have received his grace. A single stone, however beautiful, is not a temple. Only when many stones are joined together on Christ the cornerstone do they become God’s dwelling place. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you that you are a stone chosen and treasured by God—and that you have not been left in a storeroom but set into God’s building.
lessons.light: A self-centered stone wants to be a monument of its own, so that people will admire its beauty; a selfless stone gladly lets itself be set into the wall, even hidden behind other stones. The focus is Jesus: he is the cornerstone, and my position and angle must be aligned with him. This is what it means to let Jesus reign—I don’t design the church; I am built by him.
think: In 1 Peter 2:4-5, what is Jesus called? And what are we called?
Would I rather be a stone that is admired or a stone that is built in?
How can I “come to him” today and let him build me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the living stone, rejected by people but precious to God. Thank you for choosing a rough stone like me and placing me in your building. I want to come to you and let your life flow into me. Build me according to your will, so that together with my brothers and sisters I may become your spiritual house. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This morning or before bed, spend ten minutes quietly reading 1 Peter 2:4-8. Then write down the name of a member who is being built together with you at church, and pray one sentence for them.
lessons.quick: Jesus is the cornerstone; I am a living stone being built by his hands.
text: Come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.
You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
Because it is contained in Scripture, “Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen and precious. He who believes in him will not be disappointed.”
For you who believe therefore is the honor, but for those who are disobedient, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone,”
and, “a stumbling stone and a rock of offense.” For they stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed.

lessons.title: You Are God’s Temple
lessons.hear:
After moving to a new city, one brother went several years without a regular church. “I watch sermons online at home,” he said, “and I can draw near to God on a mountaintop. Why do I have to go to church?” It sounds spiritual, and part of it is true: God is everywhere, and personal intimacy with him is precious. Some members, because of health, work, or distance, can only join online for a season, and that isn’t a problem. But this brother gradually realized that his faith had become like a stone tossed into an empty field: no one knew him, no one could counsel him, and no one needed him.

In the Old Testament, God told Moses, “Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). What God longed for was never merely to meet people one by one, but to dwell “among” his people. Later Solomon built a magnificent temple, yet in his prayer he said, “Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27).

In the New Testament, God did something even more wonderful. Paul told the church in Corinth, “Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). The “you” here is plural; it refers to the whole church community. The temple God lives in today is not a building but a people joined together in Christ.

So saying “I don’t need the church” is like a stone saying, “I am a temple all by myself.” No—you are part of the temple, but not the whole temple. Paul goes on soberly: “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:17). In the Corinthian context, what was destroying God’s temple was jealousy and strife (see 1 Corinthians 3:3-4). God cares deeply about the unity of the church, because that is where he dwells.
lessons.light: Self-centered faith says, “What’s between God and me doesn’t involve anyone else.” Selfless faith says, “God dwells among us; I need my brothers and sisters, and they need me.” A changed perspective changes our mindset: we move from a private, earthly viewpoint to God’s viewpoint—his desire has always been to dwell among his people.
think: Who is the “you” in 1 Corinthians 3:16-17? Where does God dwell?
Have I ever felt that I could follow Christ without the church? What was behind that?
How can I connect more genuinely with a group of fellow members?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for longing to dwell among your people. I confess that I have wanted a faith that belongs only to me, where no one bothers me and I answer to no one. Set this stone back into your temple. Help me treasure my brothers and sisters and join with them in guarding the unity and holiness of the church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you don’t currently have a regular small group, contact a pastor or ministry leader today and ask which group you could join. If you already have one, send a message today to a member who has been coming less often: “We miss you.”
lessons.quick: God’s temple is not a building; it is us, with the Holy Spirit dwelling among us.
text: Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you?
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.

lessons.title: Fitted Together
lessons.hear:
Anyone who builds houses knows that no matter how good the stones are, if they don’t fit together, the wall will have gaps, and when the storms come, water seeps through. Describing the church as a building, Paul says, “in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21-22).

Being “fitted together” is a very practical skill, and in church life it often shows up in how we serve side by side. A choir director and a sound technician kept clashing over volume levels and the order of service. Eventually the two agreed that before every rehearsal they would pray together for five minutes and then go over the run sheet. The friction didn’t disappear completely, but they learned to make room for each other, and Sunday worship flowed more smoothly. That is two stones being fitted together as they rub against each other.

Fitting together takes three things. 1. Aligning with the same cornerstone—not with my preferences, but with the heart of Christ. 2. Being willing to have some of my rough edges worn down—not insisting that everything be done my way. 3. Being willing to be placed where no one notices—no one sees the stones at the base of a wall, yet they bear the weight of the whole wall.

Notice the words “built together.” No stone is built alone. Today’s assignment is to find a member who serves with you or is in your small group, and take the initiative to do one thing that helps you fit together better: a word of thanks, an honest conversation, an apology, or praying together. God’s house is built just like this—one stone at a time, one day at a time.
lessons.light: A proud stone refuses to be shaped and expects others to adjust to it; a humble stone is willing to adjust so that the whole wall stands firm. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the fruitfulness of service often depends on whether co-workers fit together well. People matter more than tasks—don’t wound those you are being built together with just to get a task done well.
think: In Ephesians 2:20-22, what is the foundation? Who is the cornerstone? And what are we?
In which area of service or which relationship am I not fitting well with others?
What will I do today for a co-worker or group member to help us fit together better?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the cornerstone. Help me align myself with you and not with my own preferences. I am willing to let you wear down my rough edges, and willing to be placed where no one notices. Lead me today to serve in peace and harmony with my brothers and sisters, so that your temple may steadily be built up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a member who serves with you or is in your small group. Thank them specifically for something they have done, and ask, “Is there anything I could do to work with you better?” Then pray together.
lessons.quick: Stones fit together when they align with Christ and make room for one another.
text: being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone;
in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.

lessons.title: Stones Shaped at the Quarry
lessons.hear:
When Solomon built the temple, there was a curious detail: “The house, when it was under construction, was built of stone prepared at the quarry; and no hammer or ax or any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was under construction” (1 Kings 6:7). The stones were shaped at the quarry first; at the building site they only needed to be set in place. In other words, the chiseling happened out of sight—and it was often uncomfortable.

Peter was one of those chiseled stones. The first time he met Jesus, the Lord looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42)—and Cephas means “rock.” Yet as he followed the Lord, this stone kept showing its rough edges: impulsive, quick to speak, eager for a seat of honor, and on the most crucial night of all, he denied the Lord three times. Jesus knew all of this in advance, yet he told him, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). After the resurrection, on the lakeshore, the Lord asked him three times whether he loved him and restored him to the work of shepherding the flock (see John 21:15-17).

In the church, God often uses fellow members as his chisel: a blunt elder, an arrangement that didn’t go as you hoped, a misunderstanding while serving. The self-centered reaction is, “Why should I have to put up with this?”—and sometimes simply walking away. The selfless reaction is to ask, “Lord, what rough edge do you want to wear away from me through this?” Of course, being chiseled does not mean enduring abuse of power or harm; when that happens, you should seek help from someone you trust.

Quietly examine yourself: What recently made me feel bumped, scraped, or offended? Did I run away, or did I let God shape me through it? Correction doesn’t mean pretending it doesn’t hurt; it means bringing the pain to the Lord, admitting my own rough edges, and trusting that he is shaping me into something useful.
lessons.light: A proud stone refuses to be chiseled and always thinks the problem is the chisel; a humble stone admits its rough edges and lets God trim them. Review and adjustment is the most painful yet most crucial stage of the eight steps: God is not trying to destroy me, but to set me, selflessly, in the most fitting place in his temple.
think: From John 1:42 to Luke 22:32, how does Jesus view Peter as a stone?
What recently made me feel “chiseled”? What was my first reaction?
Which rough edge will I bring to the Lord and ask him to trim?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, when you saw Simon you called him a rock, and when you see me you see what you intend to make of me. I confess that I often resist your chisel and blame the people around me. Forgive my pride, give me courage to face my own rough edges, and when I fall, help me turn back like Peter and strengthen my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down a recent situation at church that made you uncomfortable. Honestly note your own part in it (your attitude, words, or expectations), confess it to the Lord, and consider whether you need to say sorry to someone.
lessons.quick: God uses fellow members as his chisel to shape me into a living stone that fits.
text: One of the two who heard John and followed him was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas” (which is by interpretation, Peter).

lessons.title: A Royal Priesthood
lessons.hear:
This week we have seen that Jesus is the living stone and the cornerstone; that we are living stones who together become God’s temple; that stones must be fitted together; and that God shapes us with his chisel. Now let’s gather all of this into another of Peter’s sentences: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9).

In the Old Testament, only Aaron’s descendants could serve as priests in the sanctuary. But in the New Testament, every believer is a priest. Priests do two things. Toward God, they “offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God” (1 Peter 2:5)—praise, prayer, and the offering of themselves. Toward people, they bring God to them—interceding for them and proclaiming God’s excellence. Different traditions arrange church offices in different ways, but “the priesthood of all believers” reminds us that serving God is not the privilege of a select few.

The “proclaiming” Peter speaks of doesn’t necessarily mean preaching from a platform. It might mean sharing in your small group how God chiseled and built you this week. It might mean telling a newcomer, “This place isn’t perfect, but God really does dwell among us.” Or it might mean bringing a young person alongside you in ministry, so that they, too, become a living stone.

A temple is not built in a day; it rises one stone after another. You are being built so that you can help others be built. Today, tell one person what you received this week, and invite them to come to the Lord and become a living stone in God’s temple.
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication. A stone can occupy only one place, but a priest can bring many people to God. A selfless priest doesn’t proclaim for the sake of their own reputation, but so that people see the excellence of the God who called us. All glory goes to God—this is where the Way of Service leads.
think: What four titles does 1 Peter 2:9-10 use to describe God’s people?
What work has God done in this stone of mine this week?
With whom will I share what I received, inviting them to be built up together with us?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for calling me—once not even counted among your people—into your marvelous light and making me a royal priest. Help me offer you praise and prayer every day, and give me courage to proclaim your excellence to others. May the people I influence also become living stones in your temple. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find your spiritual companion or a small group member. Spend five minutes sharing one way God “chiseled” and built you this week, then pray for them, asking God to help them find their own place to be built up in the church.
lessons.quick: I am being built, and I help others be built; I am a priest called by God.
text: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
In the past, you were not a people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.

weeks.title: Bride of Christ, Embassy of the Kingdom
weeks.keyText: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
weeks.theme: Christ gave himself up for the church; we are his beloved bride and the ambassadors he sends into the world.
group: Read Ephesians 5:25-32. How does Christ love the church? Which verb moves you most?
When you talk about the church, does your tone sound like you are speaking of a beloved bride or a disappointing institution?
To which friend who doesn’t yet believe will you be Christ’s ambassador this week? Name the person and one thing you will do.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, come to worship like a bride getting ready to meet her groom: go to bed a little earlier the night before, quietly confess your sins, and prepare a clean heart. During the service, notice how Christ speaks to you through the songs, the Word, and the members of his body. Afterward, pray for a relative or friend who doesn’t yet believe, and ask God for an opportunity to be his ambassador.

lessons.title: Christ Loved the Church and Gave Himself for Her
lessons.hear:
While teaching about marriage, Paul suddenly turns his gaze to a greater mystery: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). Then he concludes, “This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly” (Ephesians 5:32). Human marriage, it turns out, is a painting—and its subject is the love between Christ and the church.

In this passage, Christ does a whole series of things for the church. He gave himself up for her—this is the love of the cross. He didn’t love his bride because she was beautiful; he laid down his life for her while she was still unlovely. He cleanses her “by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:26)—he not only accepts us as we are but also makes us new. He intends to “present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27)—in his heart he already sees the church’s future beauty. And he “nourishes and cherishes” her (Ephesians 5:29), the way a person carefully looks after their own body.

We often look at the church through our own eyes: conflict here, weakness there, pastors with flaws, members who are immature. But Christ sees the church differently. In the Old Testament, the prophets were already using marriage to describe God’s relationship with his people: “As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). When a bridegroom looks at his bride, he sees not only today’s wrinkles but also her radiance on the wedding day.

This gives us two reminders. First, when you feel unworthy, or feel the church isn’t good enough, remember that Christ has already given himself up for her—and for you. Second, when you are tempted to criticize the church, remember that you are speaking about the bride Christ loves. We can name problems honestly, but as we speak, our hearts should love her the way the Bridegroom does.
lessons.light: A self-centered person looks at the church and sees only wrinkles and spots; a selfless person learns to see her through Christ’s eyes—not denying the problems, but holding them with love and hope. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Christ gave himself up for the church, and we too are called to pour ourselves out for the church he loves.
think: In Ephesians 5:25-29, what does Christ do for the church?
When I talk about the church, do I sound more like the bridegroom or like a critic?
What can I lay down for the church this week—my time, my opinions, or my pride?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving yourself up for me while I was still unlovely, and for giving yourself up for your church. Forgive me for so often speaking about the bride you love with contempt or indifference. Put your eyes into my heart, so that I love what you love and gladly pour myself out for your church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list three things about your church you are thankful for and offer thanks to the Lord. Then share one of them in your small group chat or with a fellow member.
lessons.quick: The church I talk about is the bride for whom Christ laid down his life.
text: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word,
that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without defect.
Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself.
For no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly,
because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.
“For this cause a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his wife. Then the two will become one flesh.”
This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly.

lessons.title: The Gates of Hades Will Not Prevail
lessons.hear:
After living through a church split and watching familiar faces leave one by one, a sister said in discouragement, “I guess this is just what church is like. It won’t last much longer.” That feeling is real. We see some churches in decline, scandals spreading, young people who leave and never come back, and it’s easy to conclude that the church is a weak institution slowly withering away.

But listen to what Jesus says. Peter recognized him: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Jesus replied, “On this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). Different traditions understand “this rock” in different ways, but several things are clear. The church is “my” church—it belongs to Christ. “I will build”—he himself is doing the work. And the gates of Hades will not prevail against it—the final victory is his.

This is moving from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from the temporary to the eternal. A local church may rise or decline; a group of believers may fail or repent. But throughout history, Christ’s church has passed again and again through persecution, heresy, corruption, and division, yet it has never been wiped out—instead, it has spread to every corner of the world.

Jesus also said he would give his disciples “the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven” (Matthew 16:19). The church is not a group barely surviving in a corner; it is the outpost and embassy of God’s kingdom on earth, carrying the good news of the kingdom and proclaiming that sins are forgiven and captives are set free. So when you sigh over the church’s weakness, don’t despair. The Lord who said “I will build” is still building his church today—and he invites you to join him in the work.
lessons.light: A self-centered person sees the church’s rise and fall as human success or failure, and so easily becomes proud—or despairs. Those who let Jesus reign know that the church is his and that he builds it. Our focus is on Jesus, not on circumstances: however dark things become, the gates of Hades cannot prevail against his church. All I need to do is stand faithfully where he has placed me.
think: In Matthew 16:18, what does Jesus declare about the church?
Do I carry a disappointed, even pessimistic, view of the church in my heart?
How can I look at my own church as “Christ’s church”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Thank you for saying that you will build your church and the gates of Hades will not prevail against her. I confess I am often discouraged by the weakness I see. Renew my vision so I can see that you are still at work, and give me faith to labor with you in this imperfect church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pray for one minute for your church and one minute for your pastors and ministry team, declaring, “Lord, this is your church, and you will surely build her.” If someone voices discouragement about the church to you, gently share Matthew 16:18 with them.
lessons.quick: The church belongs to Christ; he builds it himself, and Hades cannot prevail.
text: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.
I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.”

lessons.title: Ambassadors for Christ
lessons.hear:
When you walk into a nation’s embassy, you are still on foreign soil, yet it feels as if you have stepped into that country: its flag hangs there, its language is spoken, and its rules are followed. An ambassador’s job is not to promote himself but to speak on behalf of his nation.

Paul says, “We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The church is the embassy of God’s kingdom on earth, and every Christian is an ambassador. Here is our identity: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Here is our mission: God “gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). Paul also reminds us, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20)—we live on earth, but we carry heaven’s passport.

An ambassador’s life faces two directions. Outwardly, we represent Christ by urging people to be reconciled to God: at work, at family gatherings, in our neighborhoods, letting people see through our lives and words what the kingdom of heaven looks like. Inwardly, the people in the embassy must first live by the ways of their homeland. If a church is full of mutual accusation and people who won’t speak to one another, the world walks in and sees not the kingdom of heaven but just a copy of this world.

So today’s practice has two steps. First, do one thing within the church that brings reconciliation: take the initiative to greet a member with whom your relationship has grown cold. Second, do one thing outward as an ambassador: pray for a relative or friend who doesn’t yet believe, and look for a chance to invite them to a service or small group. You don’t need to say much—just sincerely speak one sentence on behalf of your King: “I would really love for you to know my Lord.”
lessons.light: An ambassador’s greatest temptation is to make himself the main character and speak in his own name. A selfless ambassador knows that every word and action represents the King who sent him. Let Jesus reign and let Jesus receive all the glory—the embassy flies his flag, not mine. Only when we first live out reconciliation within the church can we bring the gospel of reconciliation to the world.
think: In 2 Corinthians 5:17-21, what ministry has God entrusted to us?
Can others tell from my words and actions that I am a citizen of heaven?
To which unbelieving friend or family member will I be Christ’s ambassador this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for reconciling me to yourself through Christ and entrusting me with the ministry of reconciliation. Help me first live out reconciliation in the church, and give me courage and gentleness to speak for you among my family, colleagues, and friends. Let people see in me what your kingdom looks like. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of a relative or friend who doesn’t yet believe, and pray for them. Sometime this week, invite them for coffee or send them a caring message, and if the opportunity arises, invite them to a small group or Sunday service.
lessons.quick: The church is the embassy of God’s kingdom, and I am Christ’s ambassador.
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

lessons.title: Return to Your First Love
lessons.hear:
Hosea was a prophet, yet God let him go through a heartbreaking marriage: his wife left him again and again for the arms of other men. Through this, God showed Israel how they had been treating him—abandoning the Husband who loved them to chase after other gods. But astonishingly, God’s response was not rejection but restoration: “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her” (Hosea 2:14). And again: “I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion” (Hosea 2:19).

The church is the bride of Christ, and each of us is part of that bride. The bride’s greatest danger is often not persecution from outside but a heart drawn to other things: success, reputation, comfort, numbers—even ministry itself. James puts it strongly: “Don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?” (James 4:4).

Quietly examine yourself: Is my love for the Lord still as fervent as it was at first? Has anything taken his place in my heart? When I come to church, is it to meet the Bridegroom—or only to see friends, fulfill obligations, and get ministry done? One ministry team member who had been busy at church for years suddenly realized one day that it had been a long time since he had prayed quietly simply because he loved the Lord. Everything he did was “for the Lord,” but very little of it was “with the Lord.”

The way to correct course is to return to the wilderness—not a place of punishment, but the place where God “speaks tenderly.” Set aside some of the busyness and come back quietly before the Lord, like a bride hearing her Bridegroom’s voice again. God promises to give there “the valley of Achor for a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15)—even the valley of failure can become a door of hope.
lessons.light: Self-centered service can quietly take the Bridegroom’s place, leaving us busy “for the Lord” but forgetting to be “with the Lord.” A selfless bride turns her focus back to Jesus: God first, then people, then tasks. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—when love for the Lord is restored, service no longer becomes a burden.
think: In Hosea 2:14-20, what words does God use to describe how he will betroth Israel?
What has recently crept in to take the Lord’s place in my heart?
How can I return to the wilderness this week to meet with the Lord alone?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are my Bridegroom, and you have never forsaken me. I confess that my heart is often drawn to other things, and even my service has taken the place of intimacy with you. Lead me once again into the wilderness and speak tenderly to me. Bring me back to my first love, and turn my valley of failure into a door of hope. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose one evening this week to switch off your phone for thirty minutes—not to prepare for ministry, but simply to read Hosea 2:14-20 and tell the Lord you love him. Write down one thing he reminds you to let go of.
lessons.quick: What the bride needs most is not more busyness, but to return to her Bridegroom.
text: “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
It will be in that day,” says the LORD, “that you will call me ‘my husband,’ and no longer call me ‘my master.’
For I will take away the names of the Baals out of her mouth, and they will no longer be mentioned by name.

In that day I will make a covenant for them with the animals of the field, and with the birds of the sky, and with the creeping things of the ground. I will break the bow, the sword, and the battle out of the land, and will make them lie down safely.
I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.
I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know the LORD.

lessons.title: The Bride Also Says, “Come!”
lessons.hear:
The Bible begins with a newlywed couple in the Garden of Eden and ends with the wedding feast of the Lamb. John heard the voice of a great multitude in heaven: “Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). This is the church’s destiny: not decline, but a wedding.

This week we have seen two glorious pictures of the church. She is the bride of Christ: loved by him, cleansed by him, getting ready for his return. She is also the embassy of God’s kingdom: serving as Christ’s ambassadors in this world, declaring that the gates of Hades will not prevail against her. These two pictures belong together. While the bride waits for her Bridegroom, she doesn’t shut the door and simply make herself beautiful; she goes out to invite more people to the wedding feast.

How does the bride make herself ready? The passage says, “It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen: for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints” (Revelation 19:8). The garment is freely given by grace, yet it is also worn, stitch by stitch, in everyday life: every act of forgiveness, every act of service, every time we lay ourselves down for a fellow member, we are preparing for that day.

The last chapter of the Bible says, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ He who hears, let him say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17). To multiply is to join this invitation. Today, pass on what you received this week to two people. Tell a fellow member, “We are the bride Christ loves—let’s get ready together!” And tell a friend who doesn’t yet believe, “There’s a wedding feast coming, and I’d really love for you to be there.”
lessons.light: Changing a mindset must finally lead to multiplication. The bride does not admire herself in isolation; she joins the Spirit in saying, “Come!” Moving from the temporary to the eternal: when I remember that the church’s destiny is the wedding feast of the Lamb, today’s hurts and sacrifices take on meaning. Everything I do is so that Jesus may receive all the glory.
think: In Revelation 19:6-9, how does the bride make herself ready?
How has my view of the church changed this week?
To which fellow member and which unbelieving friend will I say, “Come!”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, we wait for your return. Thank you for making your church your bride and giving her bright, pure linen to wear. Help me prepare myself through daily forgiveness, service, and self-giving, and let me join the Spirit in saying, “Come!”—inviting many more to your wedding feast. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, share with your spiritual companion the verse that moved you most this week, and pray together for a friend who doesn’t yet believe. Sometime this week, extend a specific invitation to that friend.
lessons.quick: The bride makes herself ready—and joins the Spirit in saying, “Come!”
text: I heard something like the voice of a great multitude, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of mighty thunders, saying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns!
Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.”
It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.
He said to me, “Write, ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.’” He said to me, “These are true words of God.”

weeks.title: I Don’t Go to Church—I Am the Church
weeks.keyText: so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
weeks.theme: The church is not a place I visit once a week but who I am in Christ every day.
group: Read Romans 12:3-8. Which of the gifts Paul lists reminds you of yourself or someone around you?
Are you usually more like someone who “goes to church” or someone who “is the church”? Can you give an example from everyday life?
This week, will each of us commit to doing one concrete thing for a fellow member outside of Sunday?
weeks.sunday: Before you leave home this Sunday, pray: “Lord, I am not going to attend a meeting; I am bringing a part of your body with me.” Come to the service with something prepared to give—a greeting, a song sung from the heart, a name to pray for. Afterward, ask yourself: What did I give to the body today?

lessons.title: Many Members, One Body
lessons.hear:
Many of us are used to saying, “I’m going to church this Sunday.” There is nothing wrong with the sentence, yet it quietly carries an idea: the church is a place, and I am a visitor. When the service ends, I “leave church” and go back to my own life.

When Paul wrote to the believers in Rome, he used a different language altogether: “so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Romans 12:5). Notice the verb. We do not “attend” one body; we “are” one body. The church is not a building we occasionally walk into; it is the identity we have been made into in Christ. Your hand never says, “I think I’ll drop by the body today.” The hand is already part of the body—and cut off from it, it cannot live.

That is why Paul first deals with how we see ourselves: do not “think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3). Neither proud nor self-despising, we measure ourselves through God’s eyes. Only then does he list the gifts: prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, showing mercy. Look closely and you will see that most of these are not titles for the pulpit but actions in ordinary life—comforting someone, sharing generously, arranging things with care, showing gentle compassion.

Even more striking, this passage comes right after Paul urges us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice (see Romans 12:1). What we offer is not one hour on Sunday but a whole person and a whole week. Your patience at the office on Tuesday, the bowl of soup you bring your neighbor on Thursday, the late-night prayer you whisper for someone in your small group—all of it is the church in action.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to rewrite your vocabulary: I don’t just go to church; I am part of the church. Wherever I am, I am joined to the body of Christ.
lessons.light: Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset: shift from “Where am I going?” to “Who am I?” The self-centered person puts church on the calendar; the selfless person lets church become an identity. The five-fold change works from the inside out—once the mindset changes, life, living, and relationships follow. Sunday is no longer the whole of our faith but the place where a week of body life flows together.
think: In Romans 12:3-8, why does Paul speak about how we view ourselves before he speaks about gifts?
When I say “go to church,” am I locking my faith inside those two hours on Sunday?
Where outside of Sunday can I live out my identity as a member of the body this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for joining me, one among many, into your body. Forgive me for so often treating the church as a place to check in once a week while forgetting that I myself am part of your body.
