Holy Spirit, help me live as a member of the body at home, at work, and in my neighborhood, so that people see you in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, add a reminder to your phone calendar on a day other than Sunday: “I am the church.” When that day comes, do one small thing for a fellow member—a word of encouragement, a phone call, or a prayer on their behalf.
lessons.quick: I don’t just go to church; in Christ, I am the church.
text: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

lessons.title: From Audience to Body Life
lessons.hear:
After moving to a new city, a young couple spent the better part of a year “trying out churches.” They compared carefully: which worship team was more professional, which pastor preached better, which children’s ministry had nicer facilities. Every Sunday the drive home sounded like a review: “The sound was too loud today.” “The sermon ran a bit long.” Six months later they had heard plenty of good sermons, yet not one person knew their names.

Then the wife gave birth and was in the hospital. A sister they had met only once, at a single small group meeting, brought soup to their home every day for a week. The wife said later, “That was when I finally understood. I had been looking for a good church, but I had never thought about becoming the church.”

Luke describes the early church this way: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42). Notice that none of these is a spectator activity. Teaching is to be held onto, fellowship is shared, bread is broken together, and prayer is offered as one. “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart” (Acts 2:46). They had both the large gathering in the temple courts and the small table at home; but what made Christ visible was a life shared day after day.

My old mindset says: the church is a place that provides spiritual services, I am the customer, and if the service is poor, I switch providers. God’s view is this: the church is a people joined together by the Holy Spirit, and I am one of them—called to receive together and to give together. The consumer asks, “What do I get?” The member asks, “What are we becoming together?”

No wonder the passage ends, “The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47). God adds new life to a living body, not to a crowd of strangers in an audience.
lessons.light: At its core the consumer mindset is self-centered: Am I satisfied? Am I getting something out of this? That is the self-centered life. Selflessness does not mean losing yourself; it means placing your “I” inside a “we.” The joy of the early church came precisely from no longer living for themselves. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than programs.
think: In Acts 2:42-47, what did the first believers do together, and which of those things did they do at home?
When I evaluate a church, what is the first thing I look at, and what does that reveal about my heart?
How can I move from being someone who is served to someone who gives alongside others?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that sometimes I act like a picky customer, grading your church by my own preferences. Forgive me. Teach me the way of the early church—steadfast, sharing life, one in heart. Let me be more than someone sitting in the audience; make me a member who gives love and gives time. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think back to the “score” you gave the last service you attended. Today, trade it for an action: message someone who sat near you that day whom you don’t know well yet, greet them, and invite them for coffee or tea.
lessons.quick: The consumer asks what I get; the member asks what we become together.
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.title: Everyone Brings a Dish
lessons.hear:
Chinese churches know the potluck well. Every family brings a dish, and the long table fills up with fried rice noodles, braised chicken drumsticks, fruit, and sweet soup. The most moving part is usually not which dish tastes best, but that everyone brought something and everyone went home full.

Paul’s description of the gatherings in Corinth has the same flavor: “When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, or has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up” (1 Corinthians 14:26). Different traditions understand the use of tongues and revelation differently, but two phrases in this verse are impossible to overlook: “each one of you” and “build each other up.” A gathering is not one or two people performing while everyone else watches. Each person brings a little of what they have received from the Lord—not to show themselves off, but to build others up.

Peter says the same: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10). What you bring need not be something for the pulpit. It might be an insight from your Bible reading this week, a small testimony of answered prayer, a caring question you have prepared for someone, or simply a heart willing to say hello first.

Today’s practice is to “prepare a dish” for the next gathering. Take a small card or open the notes app on your phone and write down three things: a verse you want to share, a person you want to care for, and a sentence you want to pray for them. Then carry it with you into your small group or Sunday service, and look for a chance to set your dish on the table.

When every person prepares like this, a gathering is no longer a program but a bountiful table. Christ is the host, and we feed one another.
lessons.light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, beginning with how you prepare before a gathering: first ask the Spirit to lay a person and a word on your heart. Denying yourself means bringing something for Jesus and for others, rather than only coming to take for yourself. This is also the practice of 920: letting the life of Christ bear fruit in the “2,” the people right beside you.
think: In 1 Corinthians 14:26, what principle for our gatherings do the words “each one of you” and “build each other up” teach me?
Do I usually show up to gatherings empty-handed, or with a heart prepared to give?
For the next gathering, which verse will I bring, and which person will I care for?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for the gifts you have placed in me—not for myself, but to build up your body. Holy Spirit, lay a fellow member and a word on my heart today, so that at the next gathering I do not come empty-handed but bring what I have received from you to build others up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write in your notes: a verse you want to share, a person you want to care for, and a prayer for them. At your next small group or Sunday gathering, share it out loud.
lessons.quick: A gathering is a potluck: everyone brings something received from the Lord.
text: What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, or has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up.
If any man speaks in another language, let there be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret.
But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself and to God.
Let two or three of the prophets speak, and let the others discern.
But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent.
For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be exhorted.
The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets,
for God is not a God of confusion but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints.

lessons.title: Busy with Our Own Houses
lessons.hear:
More than five hundred years before Christ, a group of Jewish exiles returned to Jerusalem and eagerly laid the foundation of the temple. But when they met opposition, the work stopped—and stayed stopped for more than a decade. The people had not stopped believing in God. They simply said, “The time hasn’t yet come, the time for the LORD’s house to be built” (Haggai 1:2).

So God asked a very direct question through the prophet Haggai: “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies waste?” (Haggai 1:4). They had no time to build God’s house, but they had time to finish their own homes with fine paneling. Then God said, “Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:5).

Today God’s house is no longer a stone building but a spiritual house built of living stones—his people (see 1 Peter 2:5). So this passage is not asking how much we gave to the building fund. It is asking: Where are my energy, my time, and my love going? It is easy to postpone our commitment with perfectly reasonable sentences: “I’ll serve when the kids are older.” “I’ll join a small group once my job settles down.” “I’ll care for others when my own spiritual life is in better shape.” These reasons may all be true. But if we keep waiting, “the time hasn’t yet come” becomes a way of life.

Take a quiet moment to review three things: 1. What am I deeply invested in, while remaining cool toward the needs of the body? 2. What reasons do I usually give for putting off becoming a builder? 3. Do I treat the church as a place that serves my household, rather than a home I help build?

The good news is that the story does not end with rebuke. When the people heard, they feared before the LORD, and God immediately promised, “I am with you” (Haggai 1:13). He stirred up their spirits, and they went back to work. Adjusting course does not require getting everything arranged first. It only requires responding to the Spirit’s prompting today: go up the mountain and bring back one piece of wood.
lessons.light: The self-centered life puts our own house at the center and pushes God’s house to “later.” It is not a great evil, but it is a quiet drift away from our proper place. The way to adjust is clear: first with God, then with people, then with tasks—put the body of Christ back into the priorities of daily life, and God himself will stir our hearts.
think: In Haggai 1:2-9, what reason did the people give for putting off building the temple, and how did God respond?
What “the time hasn’t yet come” sentence do I most often use to put off investing in the life of the body?
What “piece of wood” can I pick up today to begin taking part in the building?
lessons.speak: The LORD of Armies, you tell me to consider my ways, and I want to face them honestly. I am often busy renovating my own life while your house stands empty. Forgive my delays and excuses. Stir my heart so that today I answer your call and build together with my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down the “I’ll… once…” excuse you use most often. Then choose one small thing you can do today: sign up to serve once, reply to your small group leader’s invitation, or visit a member you haven’t seen in a long time.
lessons.quick: Don’t let “not yet” become a way of life; pick up a piece of wood today.
text: “This is what the LORD of Armies says: These people say, ‘The time hasn’t yet come, the time for the LORD’s house to be built.’”
Then the LORD’s word came by Haggai the prophet, saying,
“Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies waste?
Now therefore this is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Consider your ways.

You have sown much, and bring in little. You eat, but you don’t have enough. You drink, but you aren’t filled with drink. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm; and he who earns wages earns wages to put them into a bag with holes in it.’
“This is what the LORD of Armies says: ‘Consider your ways.
Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house. I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified,” says the LORD.

“You looked for much, and, behold, it came to little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why?” says the LORD of Armies, “Because of my house that lies waste, while each of you is busy with his own house.

lessons.title: The Echo That Rang Out
lessons.hear:
The church in Thessalonica was a very young church. Paul stayed there only a short time before persecution forced him to leave. By human standards they had no building, no tradition, and no fully trained leaders. Yet Paul later wrote to them, “you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7).

How did they do it? Not through a big evangelistic rally, but through a group of people who lived out being the church. They “turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Their changed lives were seen by neighbors, coworkers, and traveling merchants, and word spread from one to ten and from ten to a hundred. Paul says, “from you the word of the Lord has been declared” (1 Thessalonians 1:8). The word behind “declared” carries the sense of a sound ringing out in every direction, like an echo across a valley. A group of people who treat the church as an identity, not just a location, is itself an echo of the gospel.

Let’s chew once more on this week’s truths: we are one body in Christ—the church is who we are. The first believers shared life and were one in heart day by day; they were not an audience. When we gather, each one brings something, and everything is done to build one another up. And we must not let “the time hasn’t yet come” steal our heart for building.

Multiplication begins with one person. Think of someone near you—perhaps a newcomer to your small group, perhaps an old friend who has believed for years but has slowly grown cold, perhaps a child in your own home. Today, give them this sentence: “We don’t just go to church; we are the church.” Then invite them to do one small thing with you: pray together for a fellow member, or prepare together the “dish” you will bring to the next gathering.

When one person wakes up, the people around them will hear the echo too.
lessons.light: The eight steps reach repetition and multiplication: hear a truth once and you will forget it; live it once and you will remember it; pass it on and it takes root. The first step of 235 is to become spiritual companions with selfless people—find a companion and walk together from “going to church” to “being the church,” so that Jesus receives the glory among us.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 1:6-10, how did others come to know about the change in the Thessalonian believers?
This week, what concrete change has there been in the way I talk and think about “church”?
Whom will I invite to practice “I am the church” with me, and when will I invite them?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for showing me that I don’t just go to church; I am part of your church. Let this truth take root in my heart, and let my life become an echo through which the people around me hear the gospel. Lead me today to encourage a companion to build together with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, message a spiritual companion or someone from your small group. Share the verse that touched you most this week, and invite them to join you this week in praying for or visiting a fellow member.
lessons.quick: A people who live as the church are themselves an echo of the gospel.
text: You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we need not say anything.
For they themselves report concerning us what kind of a reception we had from you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God,
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

weeks.title: Diagnosing the Self-Centered Churchgoer
weeks.keyText: I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
weeks.theme: The root of the consumer mindset is self-centeredness, and being diagnosed is not a humiliation but the beginning of healing.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 3:1-9. How does Paul diagnose the “fleshly” symptoms of the Corinthian church?
Fault-finding, comparing, forming factions, seeking only your own benefit—which of these shows up in you most easily?
This week, will each of us choose one member we have quietly compared ourselves with or criticized, and do something to bless them?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before the service, ask the Lord to show you the scorecard you keep in your heart, and hand it over to him. During the service, don’t compare speakers or critique the songs; focus on listening for what the Holy Spirit is saying to you. Afterward, thank someone who served, telling them specifically how they helped you.

lessons.title: Who Gives the Increase?
lessons.hear:
A doctor first looks at the symptoms, then searches for the root cause. When Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, he wrote like a spiritual physician. This was a church rich in gifts, eloquence, and knowledge, yet Paul said something very heavy: “you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

The symptoms were plain. Some said, “I follow Paul,” and others, “I follow Apollos.” They rallied behind spiritual leaders like flags, comparing them and taking sides. Change the setting and it sounds very familiar: “I only listen to Pastor So-and-so.” “That small group goes deeper.” “The old team was better.” On the surface we are talking about ministry; underneath we are saying, “My preferences are the standard.”

What is the root cause? Paul calls them “babies in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1). Babies are not bad, but they are centered on their own needs—they cry when hungry and fuss when things don’t go their way. To believe for many years and still be centered on yourself is a kind of spiritual stunted growth.

Paul’s prescription is to turn our eyes from people back to God: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). The one who plants matters, and the one who waters matters, but both are only servants. The one who truly makes life grow is God. Once I grasp this, I no longer need to exalt one person or put down another. I only need to ask: How is God giving growth here? And how can I work together with him?

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to be like a good physician, shining his light gently and precisely on the root of the sickness in our hearts. Being diagnosed is not a humiliation; it is the beginning of healing.
lessons.light: The root of self-centeredness is wanting to be the center, the standard, and the king. In church it often dresses itself in spiritual clothing: “I just have high standards for the truth.” The selfless person keeps the focus on Jesus, not on people. They can appreciate the one who plants and thank the one who waters, and give all the glory to God, who gives the increase.
think: In 1 Corinthians 3:1-9, how does Paul describe his own role and that of Apollos?
Have I ever said or thought, in effect, “I follow So-and-so”?
How can I turn my focus today from people back to “God who gives the increase”?
lessons.speak: God who gives the increase, I confess that I often fix my eyes on people, lifting up those I like and ignoring those I don’t. Heal my spiritual immaturity. Turn me from being centered on myself to being centered on you. Make me a fellow worker with you, and let me give all the glory to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, thank God in prayer for two spiritual mentors or co-workers who have planted and watered in your life. Then send one of them a message of thanks, naming specifically how they helped you.
lessons.quick: Those who plant and water are servants; only God gives the increase.
text: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ.
I fed you with milk, not with solid food, for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, you aren’t ready even now,
for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?
Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him?
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.
Now he who plants and he who waters are the same, but each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.

lessons.title: Is Christ Divided?
lessons.hear:
A brother had served in his church for many years, and everyone said he was “very insightful.” In the little huddles after ministry team meetings, he would often say, “The worship at our old church had more depth.” “The new preacher is too shallow.” “I knew all along that decision would fail.” Gradually, a small group of people always sat around him. He never intended to split the church; he simply felt he was telling the truth. Then one day a newcomer asked him privately, “So how many factions are there in this church, anyway?” He was stunned.

Paul felt that same heartache when he heard the news from Corinth: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ’” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Interestingly, even “I follow Christ” had become a faction—the most spiritual slogan of all, used to separate oneself from others.

Then Paul asks, “Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). That one question turns our old mindset upside down. My old mindset says: I find fault because I have standards; I compare because I have discernment; I stay close to certain people because we are like-minded; I choose where to serve based on whether I am being fed. God’s view is this: when my preferences become the ruler by which I measure everything, fault-finding, comparing, faction-forming, and self-seeking grow naturally—and it is the body of Christ that gets hurt.

This does not mean we cannot have opinions. Biblical concerns can and should be spoken in love, in the right setting. The problem is not whether we have opinions but where they come from: are they meant to build up the body, or to prove that I am right?

May we all, like that brother, be awakened by a single question, and humbly return to the path where we “speak the same thing” and are “perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10).
lessons.light: The root of factions is self-centeredness: enlarging my preferences into “our” preferences, and then setting “us” against “them.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. The selfless person still has opinions but is not centered on self. They return to their proper place as a member and let Christ be the head—and so they can disagree without dividing.
think: In 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, what questions does Paul use to break down the quarreling?
How much of what I say is meant to build up the body, and how much to prove that I am right?
What kind of comparing or behind-the-back commentary will I stop today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, your body is not divided, yet I often use my preferences to sort people into sides. Forgive me for making fault-finding my standard and comparison my way of seeing. Holy Spirit, cleanse my thoughts and my tongue, so that when I have an opinion I speak it in love, in the right place, to build up the body and not to exalt myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, pay attention to how you talk about church. Whenever you catch yourself saying something comparing or critical, stop, silently hand that person over to the Lord, and pray a sentence of blessing over them.
lessons.quick: Christ is not divided; my preferences cannot be the body’s measuring stick.
text: Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who are from Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you.
Now I mean this, that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” and, “I follow Christ.”
Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?
I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,
so that no one should say that I had baptized you into my own name.
(I also baptized the household of Stephanas; besides them, I don’t know whether I baptized any other.)
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the Good News—not in wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ wouldn’t be made void.

lessons.title: Seeking the Good of Others
lessons.hear:
The believers in Corinth once argued endlessly over a very everyday question: Is it all right to eat meat that has been offered to idols? Those with more knowledge said, “Idols are nothing; I have freedom.” Yet those with weaker consciences stumbled because of it. Paul did not simply answer yes or no. He offered a higher principle: “‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are profitable. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good” (1 Corinthians 10:23-24).

The consumer’s question is, “What’s in this for me?” The member’s question is, “What is good for the body?” The two questions differ by only a few words, yet they produce completely different kinds of church life.

Today, let’s bring this principle down to one concrete, small thing. Here are three examples; just choose one: 1. At the service, leave the convenient seats for older people or newcomers, and sit in the front row or a corner yourself. 2. When a song is not your preferred style, sing it wholeheartedly anyway, because that song may be exactly what comforts someone else. 3. In small group, when you want to discuss something deeper, pause first and listen to the quietest member. None of these are big things, but each one takes apart, bit by bit, the habit of putting myself at the center.

Paul says of himself, “I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:33). This is not people-pleasing, because his goal is “whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). When we lay down a bit of our freedom for the sake of others, we are imitating the Lord who did not seek his own benefit but laid down his life for us.

Choose one today and quietly do it. No one needs to know; it is enough that the Lord knows.
lessons.light: To deny yourself is to live for Jesus and for others, not for yourself. This is not losing yourself, but entering a larger “we.” Every small act of yielding is practice in the selfless “0” of 920, letting the life of Christ bear fruit in the “2,” the people beside you.
think: In 1 Corinthians 10:23-33, what principle does Paul use to weigh things that are “lawful”?
In church, what preference am I least willing to lay down for others?
What concrete action will I choose today to seek the good of others?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you did not seek your own benefit; you even laid down your life for me. Yet I often insist on my own convenience and preferences in small things. Give me a heart willing to yield, so that today, in one concrete matter, I choose the good of others and your name is glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Choose one of the three examples from today’s lesson, or set one of your own, and carry it out at your next service or small group. Afterward, write one sentence: what I laid down, and what someone else gained.
lessons.quick: Don’t ask what’s in it for me; ask what is good for the body.
text: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are profitable. “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things build up.
Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.
Whatever is sold in the butcher shop, eat, asking no question for the sake of conscience,
for “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.”
But if one of those who don’t believe invites you to a meal, and you are inclined to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience.
But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” don’t eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for the sake of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, with all its fullness.”
Conscience, I say, not your own, but the other’s conscience. For why is my liberty judged by another conscience?
If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced for something I give thanks for?
Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, to Greeks, or to the assembly of God;
even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.

lessons.title: Tired of Manna
lessons.hear:
After Israel came out of Egypt, manna fell from heaven every day. It was food God himself provided—no plowing, no paying, there around the camp every morning. Scripture says it looked like bdellium, a pale, pearl-like resin; it was made into cakes, and its taste was like fresh oil. Yet before long the people began to long for the fish and melons of Egypt, weeping, “But now we have lost our appetite. There is nothing at all except this manna to look at” (Numbers 11:6).

Notice their tone. It was not that they had nothing to eat; they were tired of what they had. The most hidden form of the consumer mindset is losing our wonder at God’s provision. We have heard so many sermons that they all seem like “the same old thing.” We have been with fellow members so long that we see only their flaws. Then we start to miss our old church, our old pastor—just as Israel missed Egypt, forgetting that it had been the house of slavery.

Today, examine yourself honestly: 1. What “manna” in my church have I grown tired of lately? 2. Do I bring my complaints to God as prayer, or do I weep about them to people at the door of my tent? 3. Underneath the complaining, what am I really longing for?

We review not to condemn ourselves but to turn back. The disciples James and John were once thinking only of themselves, asking Jesus to let one sit at his right and the other at his left in his glory (see Mark 10:35-37). But the Lord did not give up on them. Years later John, who once wanted the high seat, wrote: “Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another” (1 John 4:11).

The first step in adjusting is to count the manna again: today, give thanks for one grace in your church that you have come to take for granted. Gratitude heals a critical spirit, the way polishing a pair of glasses makes old things shine again.
lessons.light: Complaining is the language of the self-centered life: it measures God’s provision by my own appetite. Pride is often not loud boasting but quiet dissatisfaction. Humility returns to its proper place and admits, “I am the one being provided for.” Give thanks in everything, give the glory to God, and the heart becomes soft again.
think: In Numbers 11:4-10, what were the Israelites complaining about, and what had they forgotten?
How many of my complaints about church do I bring to God, and how many do I tell to people?
For which grace in my church that I take for granted will I give thanks today?
lessons.speak: Faithful Father, you provide for me in the church every day, yet I so often grow tired of it, bored with it, and nostalgic for the past. Forgive my critical and complaining heart. Open my eyes again to see the manna you give through the pulpit, through fellow members, and through my small group, and fill my mouth with thanksgiving. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three graces in your church that you have come to take for granted (a sermon, a co-worker, a gathering). Thank God for each one, then pick one person connected to them and send a message thanking them.
lessons.quick: Gratitude heals a critical spirit; count the manna in your church again.
text: The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly; and the children of Israel also wept again, and said, “Who will give us meat to eat?
We remember the fish, which we ate in Egypt for nothing; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic;
but now we have lost our appetite. There is nothing at all except this manna to look at.”
The manna was like coriander seed, and it looked like bdellium.
The people went around, gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in mortars, and boiled it in pots, and made cakes of it. Its taste was like the taste of fresh oil.
When the dew fell on the camp in the night, the manna fell on it.
Moses heard the people weeping throughout their families, every man at the door of his tent; and the LORD’s anger burned greatly; and Moses was displeased.

lessons.title: People Like Timothy
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote Philippians from prison, he wanted to send someone to visit this church he loved so dearly. He looked around and said something heartbreaking: “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21). He did not mean that the others were unbelievers. He meant that when there was a price to pay, most people thought of themselves first.

But there was one exception: “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you” (Philippians 2:20). How did Timothy become that kind of person? Paul goes on: “But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.” (Philippians 2:22). Timothy was not born selfless. He was shaped, slowly, within a spiritual father-son relationship, laboring side by side with Paul.

This week we have honestly diagnosed the self-centered churchgoer: treating leaders like flags and taking sides, using our own preferences as the measuring stick, always asking first what’s in it for me, growing tired of God’s provision and doing nothing but complain. All of us carry some of these symptoms. But this week we have also seen the prescription: only God gives the increase; Christ is not divided; seek the good of others; replace criticism with gratitude.

To repeat is to take a little of this medicine every day; to multiply is to pass it on through relationships. Timothy “caught” his life from Paul. Today, think about this: Who is my Paul, and what can I learn from them? Who might be my Timothy, and what can I do together with them?

A healthy church is not one without self-centered people. It is one where more and more people are willing to hold each other up, turning together from seeking their own things to seeking the things of Jesus Christ.
lessons.light: The “3” of 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children. The selfless life is not learned in a classroom; it is passed on through laboring together. Timothy was mentored by Paul and went on to mentor others. Change begins with me, but it does not stop with me.
think: In Philippians 2:19-24, how does Paul describe the difference between Timothy and the others?
This week, which symptom of self-centeredness did I diagnose in myself?
Who might be my Timothy, and what could I invite them to do with me this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often seek my own things and not yours. Thank you for shining your light on me so gently this week—not condemning me, but giving me the medicine for healing. Make me like Timothy, truly caring for my fellow members, and give me someone to labor alongside and to pass this life on to. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, arrange with a younger or newer member to visit someone who needs care, or to serve together once this week. On the way, share one thing you received from God this week.
lessons.quick: Turn from seeking my own things to seeking the things of Jesus Christ.
text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.
Therefore I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how it will go with me.
But I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly.

weeks.title: Let Christ Reign in the Church
weeks.keyText: He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.
weeks.theme: The head of the church is not any person but Christ, and only when he reigns does the church have order and life.
group: Read Colossians 1:15-20. What place does Christ hold over all creation and in the church?
In your church life, what tends to slip quietly into the position of “head” without your noticing?
This week, will our small group practice pausing for one quiet minute to seek the Lord’s mind before every discussion of church matters?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before the service, declare: “Lord Jesus, you are the head of the church and the Lord of this gathering today.” During the service, notice the moments when you want your own preferences to be in charge. Afterward, pray for your pastors and ministry team, asking the Lord to help them—and you—gladly submit to Christ, the head.

lessons.title: Preeminent in All Things
lessons.hear:
The church in Colossae was being swayed by teaching that sounded right but wasn’t: Christ is good, but not quite enough—you also need some special knowledge, rituals, or angels as go-betweens. Paul answered with a magnificent hymn to Christ that pulls everyone’s eyes back to the center.

He says Christ is Lord of creation: “All things have been created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16). He is also the Lord who sustains: “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:17). Then Paul ties this Lord of the universe to an ordinary group of believers: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18).

Picture the solar system. All the planets circle the sun, each with its own orbit and speed, yet everything moves in order. If one planet tried to become the center, the whole system would fall into chaos. The church is like that. Christ is the center, and every person, every ministry, and every tradition revolves around him. Pastors are servants called by the Lord, co-workers are members sent by the Lord, and structures exist to serve life. They are all precious, but none of them can take the place at the center.

“In all things he might have the preeminence” means not only in the pulpit and in our songs, but also in the decisions of the ministry team, the allocation of the budget, the atmosphere of the small group, and my attitude toward another member. Christ’s preeminence is not a slogan but a question inside every concrete choice: In this matter, what does Jesus want?

And this head is the Lord who reconciled all things to God, “having made peace through the blood of his cross” (see Colossians 1:20). He does not reign by crushing people; he reigns with self-giving love. When we let him reign, we are not crushed—we are healed and set free.
lessons.light: One of the two cores of the 321 Vision is to let Jesus reign. His reign lands first not on other people but in my own heart: Have my opinions, my preferences, and my pride all bowed beneath him? When every member lets Jesus reign, the church naturally has order, because everyone is moving around the same center.
think: In Colossians 1:15-20, in what ways does Paul describe Christ’s position?
In which concrete area of church life is it hardest for me to give Christ first place?
What decision will I make today only after first asking, “What does Jesus want?”
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Creator of all things and the head of the church. I want to put you back at the center of my life, and not let my preferences, opinions, or pride sit in your place. Be preeminent in our church, so that pastors, co-workers, and every member gladly submit to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, in one church-related matter (replying to a message, preparing to serve, or joining a discussion), stop before you begin and pray one sentence: “Lord, what do you want in this?” Then act on it.
lessons.quick: Christ is the center; when everything revolves around him, the church has order.
text: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him.
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.
He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him,
and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.

lessons.title: The Throne in My Heart
lessons.hear:
John’s third letter is very short, yet it records a name that should sober us: “Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say” (3 John 9). He not only rejected the apostle’s letter; he refused to welcome the brothers himself, forbade others to welcome them, and even threw those who did out of the church.

Reading this, it is easy to picture Diotrephes as a certain type of person and then quietly point the finger at someone else. But slow down for a moment. Loving to be first is not the monopoly of any particular office; it is a tendency in every self-centered heart. It can show up in a co-worker who has served for many years, whose first reaction to newcomers is, “This is how we’ve always done things here.” It can show up in a large extended family, where every important matter must first be cleared with the family. It can even show up in a member who rarely takes part—uninvolved, yet expecting everything to go their way.

A sister who had served in children’s Sunday school for more than ten years later admitted, “I thought I was protecting the ministry. Later I realized I was protecting my position.” When she handed that position back to the Lord, began training new teachers, and let them try different approaches, she found herself freer and more joyful than before.

My old mindset says: whoever gives the most, has been around the longest, or is most capable should have the final say. God’s view is this: only Christ is first; everyone else is a brother or sister. Jesus said, “one is your master, the Christ” (Matthew 23:10). This does not deny the leadership and offices God has established. It reminds everyone who serves that leading is for serving, not for being first.

John’s exhortation is gentle: “don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good” (3 John 11). Today, let’s not rush to identify who the Diotrephes is. Let’s first ask: Is there a little Diotrephes in my own heart?
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power, and in church its most common form is loving to be first. Humility is laying power down and returning to our proper place: letting people be people and letting God be God. If you truly face spiritual abuse, you can and should seek help from a trusted third party. But for my own part, the first thing to deal with is the chair in my heart that I long to sit in.
think: In 3 John 9-11, how did Diotrephes’ love of being first show itself?
Where I serve or take part, am I also protecting my own position?
What position can I hand back to the Lord, or give up to someone else, today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you alone are the head of the church. I confess that there are times when I also want to be first and want others to do things my way. Tear down the throne in my heart and bring me back to my proper place as a member. Keep all who lead, as well as me, humble before you, serving rather than controlling. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of an area where you have some influence (a ministry, a group chat, or a small group). Today, take the initiative to invite a member who rarely speaks up to share their view, and listen carefully all the way to the end.
lessons.quick: Don’t rush to name the Diotrephes; first take down the throne in your own heart.
text: I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say.

Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, he doesn’t receive the brothers himself, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly.
Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God.

lessons.title: Let His Peace Rule
lessons.hear:
Letting Christ reign sounds grand, but in everyday church life it often comes down to very small moments: a message in the ministry team group chat that rubs you the wrong way, a sharp comment in small group, an arrangement you don’t agree with. In that moment, who is in charge of your heart?

Paul says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful” (Colossians 3:15). The word translated “rule” originally meant to act as an umpire in an athletic contest. When two voices are tugging inside you—one saying, “I’m going to fire back,” and the other, “Be quiet first”—let the peace that Christ has won for us blow the whistle and make the call. Paul adds that we were called “in one body,” so this peace is not only a private feeling; it is also the order of the body.

Today, let’s practice a simple “Stop, Ask, Thank”:

Stop: Before you respond, pause for ten seconds. Don’t rush to type or to speak. Ask: Ask the Lord in your heart, “In this situation, what response would let your peace rule?” You might also recall a verse, letting “the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (see Colossians 3:16). Thank: Find one thing in the situation to be grateful for, even if it is only, “Thank you, Lord, that this person is also willing to give of themselves for the church.”

Then respond. You will find that the content of your reply may not change, but its tone often does. Paul says, “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Colossians 3:17). To speak in the Lord’s name is to speak on his behalf. When we do this, Christ reigns even in a tiny group-chat message.
lessons.light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head; lead with the heart and you will find joy, lead with the head and you will find worry. Letting God’s peace be the umpire means not letting emotions or pride reign. This is change at the level of living: in our mindset we confess that Christ is the head, and in daily life we let him have the final say in every response.
think: In Colossians 3:15-17, what does Paul say should be at work in our hearts and our lives?
When was the last time I let my emotions, rather than God’s peace, be in charge?
When an uncomfortable moment comes today, how will I practice “Stop, Ask, Thank”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, let your peace rule in my heart today. When I want to respond in a hurry or prove myself, remind me to stop and ask you, and to find something to be thankful for. Let every word and every message I send be spoken in your name, so that your body is built up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, before replying to any church group chat or any member’s message, practice “Stop, Ask, Thank”: stop for ten seconds, ask the Lord one question, find one thing to be thankful for—and only then press send.
lessons.quick: Stop, Ask, Thank—let his peace blow the whistle in your heart.
text: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

lessons.title: A King Like the Nations
lessons.hear:
The elders of Israel came to the aging Samuel with what seemed a reasonable request: “Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations” (1 Samuel 8:5). Samuel’s sons really did not walk in his ways, so the people’s worry was not groundless. But God said to Samuel, “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7).

The problem was not whether to have leaders. God later chose David himself and shepherded his people through a king after his own heart. The problem was in four words: “like all the nations.” They wanted someone they could see, touch, and lean on to take the place of the God who is unseen yet truly reigns.

The church today can face the same temptation, and it usually comes from two directions. One is pushing a person onto the throne: we expect a certain pastor or leader to be good at everything and put our faith in their gifts and charisma; the moment they disappoint us, we turn to blaming them or simply leave. That is unfair to us and unfair to them, because we have placed on one person a weight only Christ can carry. The other direction is sitting on the throne ourselves: we would never say it out loud, but in our hearts we are certain that our judgment is the final standard.

Take time quietly to review: Are my expectations of the church built on Christ, or on a person, a program, or a model of success that is “like other churches”? When people disappoint me, does my faith still stand?

The way to adjust is not to do without leaders or to trust no one. It is to give the throne back to Christ and then see people rightly: honor the leadership God has established, pray for them, and allow them to be weak. God did not abandon his people because of their mistake; in the end he sent the true King, Jesus, who laid down his life for his people.
lessons.light: Pushing others onto the throne and climbing onto it ourselves both let something else reign in place of Jesus. The first is relying on people; the second is pride; both leave our proper place. A church where Jesus reigns honors its leaders without idolizing them and follows their direction without following blindly, because everyone’s eyes are on the same King.
think: In 1 Samuel 8:4-9, how did God view the people’s demand for a king?
Have I put a person or a model in the seat that only Christ can occupy?
When a leader disappoints me, how will I place my faith back on Christ?
lessons.speak: King of heaven, I confess that sometimes I want a person I can see to take your place, and sometimes I want to be king myself. Forgive me for putting the weight in the wrong place. I choose to honor the leaders you have established, to pray for them, and to accept their weaknesses—but my faith rests on you alone. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes praying for your pastor or a ministry leader who leads you. Ask the Lord to strengthen them, and to help you not place on them a weight only Christ can carry.
lessons.quick: Honor your leaders, but the throne belongs to Christ alone.
text: Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together and came to Samuel to Ramah.
They said to him, “Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prayed to the LORD.
The LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.
According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, in that they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they also do to you.
Now therefore, listen to their voice. However, you shall protest solemnly to them, and shall show them the way of the king who will reign over them.”

lessons.title: Only the Lamb Is Worthy
lessons.hear:
In his vision John saw the throne in heaven. The living creatures and the elders around it fell down, and countless thousands of angels said with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12).

This is the whole universe’s answer to the question: Who is worthy to reign? Not the strongest, not the richest, not the most eloquent, but the Lamb who was killed. His right to reign comes from his self-giving. With his own blood he “bought us for God … out of every tribe, language, people, and nation” (Revelation 5:9). People who had nothing to do with one another became one people because of one King.

This week we have seen the same thing again and again: Christ is the head of the body, the church, preeminent in all things; the little Diotrephes in my heart, who loves to be first, needs to be taken down; we let God’s peace rule in every small response; and we must not let a visible person or a successful model replace the King who is unseen yet real.

The worship of heaven is the direction for the church on earth. Every time we gather, we are rehearsing for that day: no one competing for position, and all the glory going to the Lamb. This is the very heart of the 321 Vision—let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Multiplying what you have received can begin in very small places. At dinner, ask your family or roommates one question: “In what situation today did Jesus reign?” In your small group, suggest that before discussing any church matter, everyone first be quiet together and seek the Lord’s mind together. As more and more people do this, the church on earth will look more and more like heaven.
lessons.light: The two cores—let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory—are really one: the throne is his, and so is the glory. The selfless person gladly turns the applause toward the Lamb. As we pass this way of seeing on to the next person, “Let your Kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10) is fulfilled little by little among us.
think: In Revelation 5:9-13, why is the Lamb worthy of all honor and glory?
This week, in what situation did I experience letting Jesus reign?
How will I lead others at home or in my small group to practice letting Jesus reign together?
lessons.speak: Lamb who was killed, you are worthy of power, honor, glory, and blessing. Today I give the throne and the glory to you. Make our church more and more like the worship of heaven, where no one competes for position and all of us lift you up together; and use me to pass this vision on to those around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight at dinner or before bed, ask a family member, roommate, or companion: “In what situation today did Jesus reign?” Share your own answer first, then listen to theirs, and finish by praying together.
lessons.quick: Only the Lamb is worthy to reign; the throne and the glory are his.
text: They sang a new song, saying, “You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals, for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation,
and made us kings and priests to our God; and we will reign on the earth.”
I looked, and I heard something like a voice of many angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders. The number of them was ten thousands of ten thousands, and thousands of thousands,
saying with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!”

I heard every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, and everything in them, saying, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!”

weeks.title: Seeing the Church Through God’s Eyes
weeks.keyText: to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
weeks.theme: Though imperfect, the church is the display of God’s manifold wisdom and the vessel in which Christ is glorified.
group: Read Ephesians 3:8-13. Through the church, what does God want to make known, and to whom?
Which lens do you most easily use to look at the church: disappointment, criticism, indifference, or hope?
This week, will each of us write down three things God has done in our church and share them with one another in small group or after Sunday service?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before you sit down, ask the Lord for a new pair of eyes. During the service, try to see every brother and sister around you as a work of God’s wisdom—including the ones you don’t particularly appreciate. Afterward, tell God about one grace you saw in this imperfect church.

lessons.title: A Display of God’s Manifold Wisdom
lessons.hear:
When we look at the church, what we usually see is very earthly: Is attendance growing? Is the budget enough? What is the ministry team arguing about this time? What hurtful thing has that member said now? All of this is real. But if this is all we see, the more we look, the more discouraged we become.

Paul wrote Ephesians from prison, in circumstances far harder than ours, yet his vision was far higher. He says God entrusted a mystery to him, “to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 3:10). Picture the scene: the whole heavenly realm is watching, and what God uses to display his wisdom is not the majestic stars but the church—a company of sinners who have received grace.

The word “manifold” carries the sense of many-colored, richly varied, like a tapestry woven from threads of countless colors. In that day, no two groups were less likely to sit together than Jews and Gentiles; yet in Christ they became one body. It is the same today: people of different ages, different accents, different backgrounds, even different convictions gather around the same Lord’s Table because of the same Lord. That in itself is a work of God’s wisdom.

And when Paul says this, he does not place himself on high: “To me, the very least of all saints, was this grace given” (Ephesians 3:8). His way of seeing the church started from grace; he knew he too was a thread that grace had picked up.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to lift your eyes from earth to heaven. Your church may not be large, and it is certainly not perfect, but it has an audience in heaven. It is a tapestry God is still weaving—and you are one of its threads.
lessons.light: Change your viewpoint and you change your mindset: from a human viewpoint to God’s, from earth to heaven. The self-centered eye sees only what dissatisfies me about the church; the eye that starts from grace sees God at work in it. When I admit that I am the very least of all, I no longer look down on the church from above.
think: In Ephesians 3:8-13, what does God want to make known through the church, and to whom?
When I look at my church, what do I see most often, and what do I see least?
In which fellow member can I see a work of God’s wisdom today?
lessons.speak: Father, open my eyes to see your church through your eyes. I often see only problems and flaws, forgetting that through this company of people who have received grace you are displaying your wisdom. I too am a thread your grace picked up; may I gladly take my place in the tapestry you are weaving. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the names of three members of your church whose backgrounds are very different from yours. For each one, write a sentence: “What has God displayed in this person?” Then thank God for them.
lessons.quick: The imperfect church is a many-colored tapestry God is still weaving.
text: To me, the very least of all saints, was this grace given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ,
and to make all men see what is the administration of the mystery which for ages has been hidden in God, who created all things through Jesus Christ,
to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places,
according to the eternal purpose which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.
In him we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him.
Therefore I ask that you may not lose heart at my troubles for you, which are your glory.

lessons.title: The Lord Who Walks Among the Lampstands
lessons.hear:
A sister lived through a church split. She watched co-workers who had trusted each other argue in meetings; the words in the group chat grew uglier and uglier, until finally a group of people left in anger. She didn’t take sides; her heart simply broke. Since then she has only watched sermons online at home. She tells her friends, “I still love Jesus. I just don’t want to go to church anymore.”

Many people carry similar wounds. These wounds are real; they need time, and they deserve gentle companionship. But beneath the wound there is often a hidden belief: the church has disappointed me, so Jesus has probably left it too.

The vision John saw on the island of Patmos gives a different answer: “among the lamp stands was one like a son of man” (Revelation 1:13). The Lord said, “The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies” (Revelation 1:20). These seven churches were not perfect. In the letters that follow, one has left its first love, one tolerates false teaching, and one is lukewarm. Yet the risen Lord does not stand at a distance criticizing them. He walks among the lampstands, holding in his right hand the seven stars, the angels of the churches.

“His eyes were like a flame of fire” (Revelation 1:14). He sees everything clearly; he rebukes, he disciplines, and he heals. This gives us a double freedom. First, we do not have to be the church’s judge, because the Lord himself is watching over it. Second, we do not have to leave in despair, because the Lord himself has not left.

My old mindset says: if the church disappoints me, that proves it isn’t worth my commitment. God’s view is this: Jesus still walks among imperfect churches; he has not given up on them, and he invites me to be there with him. When John fell down, the Lord laid his right hand on him and said, “Don’t be afraid” (Revelation 1:17). To you who have been hurt, he says the same.
lessons.light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on other people or circumstances. When I stare only at people’s failures, my faith wobbles with them; when I see the Lord walking among the lampstands, I can stand firm again. Selflessness is not pretending I wasn’t hurt. It is letting Jesus reign—entrusting even my wounds to him to heal and to judge.
think: In Revelation 1:12-20, where is the one like a son of man, and what does he hold in his hand?
Because of people’s failures, have I “shown Jesus the door” of the church as well?
If the Lord is still walking in my church, how can I respond to him today?
lessons.speak: Risen Lord, thank you for not leaving the imperfect church; you still walk among the lampstands. I place my disappointment and hurt over the church in your hands. Heal me, and search and cleanse your church yourself. As you tell me not to be afraid, give me courage to walk with your people again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you have been hurt in church, write it down today and hand it over to the Lord, then arrange to talk with a trusted spiritual mentor or companion. If not, pray today for someone who has drifted away from gatherings after being hurt, and reach out to them.
lessons.quick: The church may disappoint us, but the Lord still walks among the lampstands.
text: I turned to see the voice that spoke with me. Having turned, I saw seven golden lamp stands.
And among the lamp stands was one like a son of man, clothed with a robe reaching down to his feet, and with a golden sash around his chest.
His head and his hair were white as white wool, like snow. His eyes were like a flame of fire.
His feet were like burnished brass, as if it had been refined in a furnace. His voice was like the voice of many waters.
He had seven stars in his right hand. Out of his mouth proceeded a sharp two-edged sword. His face was like the sun shining at its brightest.
When I saw him, I fell at his feet like a dead man. He laid his right hand on me, saying, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last,
and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever. Amen. I have the keys of Death and of Hades.
Write therefore the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which will happen hereafter.

The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lamp stands is this: The seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies. The seven lamp stands are seven assemblies.

lessons.title: Back to Your First Love
lessons.hear:
The church in Ephesus was an “excellent” church. The Lord praised their works, their toil, and their perseverance. They could tell false apostles from true ones, and they labored for the Lord’s name without growing weary. By human scoring, it should have been a model church. Yet the Lord said, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4).

This gives us an important reminder: seeing the church through God’s eyes means not only seeing others’ shortcomings but also seeing our own coldness. We may do a great deal and know a great deal, yet no longer love—no longer rejoicing when a newcomer arrives, no longer weeping when a fellow member falls. Serving becomes a duty roster; gathering becomes a habit.

The Lord’s prescription has three actions: “Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5). Remember, repent, and do. Love does not come back simply by waiting for the feelings to return; it is rekindled by the Holy Spirit as we go back to doing the things we did at first.

Let’s put it into practice today. Take three minutes to remember: When you first believed, or first came to this church, what did you do that you no longer do now? Perhaps you came early to help set up chairs. Perhaps you invited friends to come. Perhaps you took notes on every sermon, or remembered the birthday of every person in your small group. Pick one of those things, and do it again this week.

At the end of every letter, the Lord says, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies” (Revelation 2:7). When one member returns to their first love, the temperature of the whole body rises with them.
lessons.light: Remembering is the reawakening of our mindset, repenting is the turning of our life, and doing is the change in our living. When our relationship with God recovers its first love, our relationships with people and our ministry regain their warmth too. Don’t grit your teeth and push on with your head; rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart to rekindle the fire.
think: In Revelation 2:1-7, what does the Lord praise in the church at Ephesus, and what does he rebuke?
In my church life, what has shifted from love into mere habit?
Which of the things I did at first can I start doing again this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you see my toil, and you also see the coldness in my heart. I confess that I have left my first love. I choose to remember, to repent, and to go back to doing the things I did at first. Holy Spirit, rekindle my love for you, for your church, and for every member. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down one thing you often did when you first came to church but no longer do. Put a day on your calendar this week to do it again—for example, arriving early to help, inviting a friend, or writing down the needs of your small group members.
lessons.quick: Remember, repent, and do—let your first love be rekindled.
text: “To the angel of the assembly in Ephesus write: “He who holds the seven stars in his right hand, he who walks among the seven golden lamp stands says these things:
“I know your works, and your toil and perseverance, and that you can’t tolerate evil men, and have tested those who call themselves apostles, and they are not, and found them false.
You have perseverance and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not grown weary.
But I have this against you, that you left your first love.
Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works; or else I am coming to you swiftly, and will move your lamp stand out of its place, unless you repent.
But this you have, that you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.
He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the assemblies. To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the Paradise of my God.

lessons.title: Am I the Only One Left?
lessons.hear:
Elijah was one of the boldest prophets of the Old Testament. On Mount Carmel he faced hundreds of the prophets of Baal alone and saw God send fire from heaven. Yet not long afterward he fled into the wilderness and hid in a cave on Mount Horeb. God asked him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9).

His answer was honest, and very weary: “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies … I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away” (1 Kings 19:10). Elijah was not lying. He really had been zealous, and he really was being persecuted. But “I, even I only, am left” was not God’s view. God told him, “Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal” (1 Kings 19:18).

After serving in church for a long time, we can walk into the same cave: “I’m the only one in this whole church who cares about the prayer meeting.” “I’m the only one who sees the problem.” “Nobody else is spiritual enough.” This kind of thinking often starts with genuine zeal, but in weariness and disappointment it slowly turns into an isolating pride. We cannot see the seven thousand—not because they don’t exist, but because our eyes have room for no one but ourselves.

Take time quietly to review: Do I often feel that I am one of the few people in the church who is truly serious? Is there a trace of self-righteousness in my discouragement? Have I gone so long without rest that my vision has narrowed?

The way God healed Elijah was very gentle. First he let him eat his fill and sleep (see 1 Kings 19:5-8). Then he spoke to him in a still small voice, gave him a new assignment, and gave him a companion, Elisha. Adjusting course begins with admitting our limits: I need rest, I need companions, and I need to see again that God has many faithful people in this church whom I do not even know.
lessons.light: A self-centered way of seeing turns the church into “just me.” The selfless person admits their limits and values the faithfulness of others, knowing that God’s work is far bigger than themselves. The first step of 235 is to find companions: God did not let Elijah serve alone, and he does not want you to carry the load alone either.
think: In 1 Kings 19:9-18, how did Elijah see his situation, and how did God respond to him?
Do I also have an “I’m the only one left” mindset in my church?
What kind of rest, companionship, or fresh perspective do I need to be renewed in strength?
lessons.speak: The LORD, I confess that sometimes I am like Elijah, feeling that I am the only one who cares, the only one who is faithful. Forgive my hidden self-righteousness, and heal my weariness. Open my eyes to see the faithful servants you have kept in the church, and give me a companion to walk the road ahead with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a member you have paid little attention to in the past but who has served quietly and faithfully. Send them a message thanking them for what they give. If you are already very weary, plan some real rest for yourself tonight.
lessons.quick: God’s faithful people in the church are far more than I can see.
text: He came to a cave there, and camped there; and behold, the LORD’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

He said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD.” Behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake a fire passed; but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
The LORD said to him, “Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.
Anoint Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel; and anoint Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel Meholah to be prophet in your place.
He who escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and he who escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.
Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him.”

lessons.title: To Him Be the Glory in the Church
lessons.hear:
Paul bows his knees in prayer for the church in Ephesus. He asks God that Christ may dwell in their hearts, that they may be rooted and grounded in love, and that they may “comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth” and “know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:18-19). Notice the words “with all the saints.” Christ’s love is too wide, too long, too high, and too deep for any one person to grasp alone. I need the side of it that you have seen, and you need the side of it that I have experienced. That is why God does not only save us as individuals; he also places us in the church.

Then Paul closes with a doxology: “to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations forever and ever. Amen” (Ephesians 3:21). God is glorified not only in heaven but also here on earth, in this company of imperfect people.

This week we have learned to see the church through God’s eyes: it is a tapestry of God’s manifold wisdom; the risen Lord still walks among the lampstands; we need to return to our first love; and the faithful people God has kept are more than we can see. This also sums up our journey from consumer to member: I am the church; I am willing to face my own self-centeredness; I let Christ reign; I see his house through God’s eyes.

“To all generations” reminds us that this way of seeing must be passed on. Today, write a short card or message to a member younger than you, or to a child in your home, and tell them: “In our church, I have seen God do this…” Name one specific grace. You are helping the next generation learn, from a young age, to see the church through God’s eyes.

As more and more people see this way, speak this way, and live this way, God—“him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us” (Ephesians 3:20)—will surely be glorified among us.
lessons.light: From the temporary to the eternal: the church that looks so ordinary today is, in eternity, the vessel in which God is glorified. The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication. Passing God’s way of seeing on to the next generation is how we build God’s system from generation to generation, so that Jesus receives all the glory.
think: In Ephesians 3:14-21, what does Paul ask God for on behalf of the church?
Over this season, what specific changes have there been in how I see the church?
To which younger member or family member will I write a card or message?
lessons.speak: Father, I bow my knees before you and thank you for letting me, with all the saints, come to know the width and length and height and depth of Christ’s love. Keep me from looking at your house with a critical and disappointed eye; let me see your works through your eyes. To you be the glory in our church, to all generations. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write a card or message to a younger member or a child in your home, naming one specific thing you have seen God accomplish in your church, and give it to them before the weekend.
lessons.quick: Grasp Christ’s love with all the saints, and let him be glorified in the church.
text: For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named,
that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,
may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth,
and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us,
to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
